source.title: What Shapes Emergent Misalignment? Insights from Training Dynamics, Model Priors, and Data
source.authors: Yu-Chen Zhang; Anietta Weckauff; Diego Garcia-Olano; Maksym Andriushchenko

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes instruction models on narrow datasets, including insecure code, and evaluates alignment-related behavior on unrelated questions. It also varies evaluation sample sizes and training schedules.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports activation-prediction and activation-overlap analyses. Those measure representation geometry or prediction rather than the free-form misaligned behavior named in the claim, so they are not behavior rows. Table 3's Pearson correlations between loss and score are not separately extracted; Table 3's average scores and Max Score Difference results are included. Some additional dataset/model plots are figure-only and listed under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes Qwen2.5 and Phi-4 chat models with LoRA on narrow data: insecure code, risky finance, bad medical, auto, and StackOverflow chemistry. It then judges free-form answers to Betley's first-plot questions and other unrelated questions using reused aligned and coherent judges plus a new harmless judge. That bears directly on V1, V2 and the training-progress part of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in-domain training loss largely governs the degree of EM and that learning schedules found no better-aligned minima at similar loss. Misaligned models' scores differ from the pre-trained model's yet correlate with them per question. Prior prompt activations partly predict per-question scores. Train and eval prompt activation shifts overlap, and the overlap tracks prompt-subspace similarity for last-token activations. Training-data-specific properties also matter.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow LoRA SFT, including insecure-code data, and unrelated-question alignment evaluation, following Betley et al. settings. It adds finance, medical, automotive, and chemistry datasets; multiple evaluation sets; harmless/aligned judges; and training-schedule, prior-activation, and activation-delta analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation sample size changes Max Score Difference substantially; the text says the Initial EM set (n = 24) is unreliable for this statistic and differences shrink at larger n. The paper also examines multiple answer formats and evaluation score types.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on benign, highest-upvoted human StackOverflow chemistry answers also induced broad misalignment in Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, though less than the downvoted data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow fine-tuning on benign, human-written domain data can still reduce broad harmlessness, so emergent misalignment is not specific to harmful training content.

fits_no_version.finding: Max Score Difference between learning-schedule runs shrinks with evaluation sample size, to 2-5 points at n>200, roughly following a power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent schedule-induced alignment differences in EM are largely evaluation-sample noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-fine-tuning prompt activations predict post-fine-tuning per-question harmlessness (Lasso CV R2 0.2-0.55). Train and eval prompt activation deltas overlap substantially.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-fine-tuning prompt representations and train-eval prompt overlap partly predict how strongly each question becomes misaligned.

record.peer_reviewed: 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML@ICML 2026)
record.problems: The Initial EM evaluation set is small (n = 24); the paper itself cautions that sample-size-sensitive Max Score Difference is unreliable at small n. Much of the broader dataset/model evidence is shown in figures rather than tabulated numerical comparisons. The authors note limited model-family coverage and resource-driven judge choices. Table 4 covers only eight questions and has no matched secure-code or class-context controls.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional training-loss plots for risky finance, automotive advice, medical advice, and insecure code in Appendix Figures 3–9; figure-only values were not separately extracted under the 60-row limit. Additional Table 3 Pearson correlations between training loss and alignment scores were omitted because the sample-size-specific averages and Max Score Difference rows were retained. Other activation analyses and figure-only steering comparisons do not directly measure the claimed behavior.

untested.parts: No secure-code or educational-insecure (class) control fine-tune; the only comparisons are the instruct and pre-trained models.
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences.
Causal mediation by a single direction or persona feature. The activation-delta overlap analyses are not causal tests of one shared direction.
Entire version: no inoculation or benign re-training.
Seed robustness, systematic coherence-filter comparison, and the onset point during training. The coherent>0.5 variant appears only in figures.

missing.what: Pearson r between training loss and alignment or harmless scores across schedule runs (e.g. Harmfulness aligned r=0.844***, Initial EM aligned r=0.834***)
Per-question harmless scores for 20 fine-tuned models, including finance vs finance-good matched controls, insecure code at 14B and 32B, medical, auto and chemistry data
Pre-trained vs misaligned Wilcoxon and Pearson significance rates across 29 model-data runs

record.verdict_notes: No inoculation or benign retraining is tested, and the Impact Statement only cites others' realignment results. Table 4's 'pre-trained' comparison uses a non-instruction-tuned base model, which is sometimes less harmless than the misaligned model. Fig. 18 heatmap rows are garbled in the text extraction; first-column values were mapped to model order, so treat those text-based verdicts cautiously. The Table 3 average scores have no untuned baseline, and the Harmfulness-question set consists of harmful requests, so those rows partly reflect harmful compliance rather than misalignment on unrelated questions.

versions.untested_parts: No matched secure-code fine-tune or insecure-code-for-a-class control is reported. The paper does not establish a direct rate of misaligned answers; Table 4 reports harmlessness scores on eight questions.
The study tests risky financial advice, bad medical advice, and human-curated chemistry data, but not harmless reward hacks or number sequences.
The paper measures activation-delta overlap and prediction, but does not test causal mediation by one linear direction or persona feature across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining intervention.

The study varies evaluation sample size and training schedules, and includes more than one model size in its reported materials, but does not report seed robustness or a systematic coherence-filter comparison. It does not isolate when during training broad misalignment first appears.
